problem: How to assess a defense's robustness when the space of possible poisoning attacks is near-limitless and testing known attacks cannot rule out new ones.
did: They built a framework that computes approximate upper bounds on worst-case loss over all attacks, paired with a candidate attack, instead of only testing hypothesized attacks.
alternatives_named: testing a defense against a number of known poisoning strategies on a clean dataset
hypothetical attacks designed to test defenses
stated_reason: It is impossible to conclude from empirical success alone that a defense that works against known attacks will not fail against a new attack.
quote: However, because of the near-limitless space of possible attacks, it is impossible to conclude from empirical success alone that a defense that works against a known set of attacks will not fail against a new attack.
title: Certified Defenses for Data Poisoning Attacks

problem: The true worst-case test loss is hard to bound directly, so a tractable surrogate is needed and its validity must be interpreted.
did: They approximated test loss by clean training loss, upper bounded it by loss on the full data, and let the defender train on all clean data, yielding a minimax loss M whose validity rests on two stated assumptions.
alternatives_named: bilevel optimization of the worst-case test loss directly
stated_reason: M admits a natural minimax formulation with duality properties that give insight into the optimal attack, whereas the direct bilevel problem is intractable in general.
quote: The approximations (i) and (iii) define the assumptions we need for our certificates to hold; as long as both approximations are valid, $\mathbf{M}$ will give an approximate upper bound on the worst-case test loss.
title: Certified Defenses for Data Poisoning Attacks

problem: How to tell how tight the computed upper bound on the minimax loss is.
did: They pair the upper bound with a candidate attack whose induced loss is a lower bound, and monitor the duality gap between them.
stated_reason: The gap between lower and upper bounds indicates the quality of the bounds, and convexity plus sublinear regret makes the gap vanish for large datasets.
quote: We can monitor the duality gap between lower and upper bounds on $\mathbf{M}$ to ascertain the quality of the bounds.
title: Certified Defenses for Data Poisoning Attacks

problem: Which kind of defender to analyze: one whose feasible set is independent of the poisoned data, or one estimated from the possibly poisoned data.
did: They analyzed both fixed oracle defenses and data-dependent defenses, using the oracle as a bound on what is achievable and then testing the realistic data-dependent case.
alternatives_named: fixed defenses
data-dependent defenses
stated_reason: Oracle defenders are not implementable but provide bounds: if even an oracle can be attacked, we should be worried; data-dependent defenders are implementable but open a new line of attack.
quote: While such defenders are not implementable in practice, they provide bounds: if even an oracle can be attacked, then we should be worried.
title: Certified Defenses for Data Poisoning Attacks

problem: Whether the candidate attack from the framework is actually strong, given that existing attack methods exist.
did: They compared their candidate attack against two baselines, gradient descent on test loss and label flipping, and also checked maximum test 0-1 error against the certificates.
alternatives_named: gradient descent on the test loss
label flipping baseline
stated_reason: Baselines provide a check that the framework's attack is strongest and that test error is consistent with the certificate; label flipping is too weak and gradient gets stuck in local minima.
quote: Our attack consistently performs strongest; label flipping seems to be too weak, while the gradient algorithm seems to get stuck in local minima.
title: Certified Defenses for Data Poisoning Attacks

problem: Whether to accept an imperfect attack and bound on text data when the integer program is too hard to solve well, leaving a large gap.
did: They accepted a valid candidate attack from the IQP solver (or randomized rounding for IMDB) with a relaxed upper bound, noting the gap, and drew conclusions from the attack's success anyway.
alternatives_named: solving the IQP exactly
relaxing the integrity constraints only
stated_reason: The integer constraints make solving expensive and IMDB was too large for Gurobi, but the attacks were still relatively successful despite the gap.
quote: Results are given in Figure 3; there is a relatively large gap between the upper bound and the attack. Despite this, the attacks are relatively successful.
title: Certified Defenses for Data Poisoning Attacks

problem: Why the IMDB dataset is far more attackable than MNIST-1-7 under the same oracle defense.
did: They inspected the geometry of the feasible set (Figure 1) and attributed the difference to high dimensionality and many irrelevant features enlarging the feasible set without separating the classes.
stated_reason: Irrelevant features increase the size of F without a corresponding increase in class separation, so the defense places few constraints on the attacker.
quote: This seems to be a consequence of the high dimensionality of IMDB and the large number of irrelevant features, which increase the size of $\mathcal{F}$ without a corresponding increase in separation between the classes.
title: Certified Defenses for Data Poisoning Attacks

problem: How strongly to state what the certificates guarantee, given they must be computed on clean data and rest on approximations.
did: They framed the bounds as a design-stage assessment tool modulo approximations, explicitly not a guarantee for a deployed algorithm.
alternatives_named: guaranteeing performance of a deployed learning algorithm
stated_reason: The method needs to be run on the clean data, which presumably would not be available at deployment time.
quote: We stress that our bounds are meant to be used as a way to assess defense strategies in the design stage, rather than guaranteeing performance of a deployed learning algorithm
title: Certified Defenses for Data Poisoning Attacks

problem: How to illustrate the troubling trends in ML scholarship with concrete examples without unfairly harming junior researchers.
did: They chose examples preferentially from their own work and from well-established researchers and institutions, and kept examples short and specific.
alternatives_named: singling out junior students
stated_reason: To avoid singling out junior students who may face consequences and lack the opportunity to reply symmetrically.
quote: our guiding principles are to (i) implicate ourselves, and (ii) to preferentially select from the work of better-established researchers and institutions that we admire, to avoid singling out junior students for whom inclusion in this discussion might have consequences
title: Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship

problem: How strongly to assert that the four patterns constitute a rising trend and to claim their causes, given limited evidence.
did: They explicitly framed the causal factors as speculation and said they suspect, rather than demonstrate, that the patterns are on the rise.
stated_reason: The causes are uncertain and the paper's suggestions are based on personal experience and impressions.
quote: We speculate that these patterns are on the rise and suspect several possible causal factors: complacency in the face of progress, the rapid expansion of the community, the consequent thinness of the reviewer pool, and misaligned incentives of scholarship vs. short-term measures of success.
title: Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship

problem: How to interpret an ambiguous quantitative claim about local minima in high-dimensional Gaussian random fields that is cited without a specific theorem.
did: They offered their own reading of the claim as a numerical statement about typical parameter settings rather than a claim that the gap vanishes in high dimensions, and recommended a formal statement.
alternatives_named: a claim that the gap vanishes in high dimensions
stated_reason: Absent a specific theorem it is difficult to verify the result or determine its precise content.
quote: Our understanding is that it is partially a numerical claim that the gap is small for typical settings of the problem parameters, as opposed to a claim that the gap vanishes in high dimensions.
title: Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship

problem: What evidence authors should gather to understand the sources of empirical gains beyond headline performance numbers.
did: They recommend error analysis, ablation studies, and robustness checks (to hyper-parameters and ideally datasets) as standard practices, while noting ablation alone is neither necessary nor sufficient.
alternatives_named: raw headline numbers
ablation studies
robustness checks
qualitative error analysis
stated_reason: Raw headline numbers provide limited value for scientific progress absent insight into what drives them.
quote: Three practices that are common in the strongest empirical papers are error analysis, ablation studies, and robustness checks (to e.g. choice of hyper-parameters, as well as ideally to choice of dataset). These practices can be adopted by everyone
title: Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship

problem: How reviewers should decide whether to accept papers that combine many untested ideas with improved results versus simpler papers with negative results.
did: They propose reviewers ask whether they would have accepted the paper if the authors had done a worse job, favoring simple ideas with negative results over unablated multi-idea papers.
alternatives_named: accepting papers on strong quantitative findings alone
stated_reason: It sets better incentives for authors by rewarding rigor rather than apparent technical novelty.
quote: Reviewers can set better incentives by asking: "Might I have accepted this paper if the authors had done a worse job?" For instance, a paper describing a simple idea that leads to improved performance, together with two negative results, should be judged more favorably
title: Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship

problem: How to interpret the case of the ImageNet breakthrough paper that proposed multiple techniques without ablations, which seems to counter their call for ablations.
did: They conceded that in that case skipping ablations may have been justified given the significance of the results and the computational cost.
alternatives_named: waiting for ablations to complete
stated_reason: The results were so significant and experiments so expensive that waiting for ablations was perhaps not worth the cost to the community.
quote: However, at the time the results were so significant and the experiments so computationally expensive to run that waiting for ablations to complete was perhaps not worth the cost to the community.
title: Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship

problem: How strongly to frame their proposed standards given counterarguments that high standards could slow research or impede speculative ideas.
did: They presented the standards as strong heuristics rather than unbreakable rules, allowing an idea to be shared even if heuristics are set aside.
alternatives_named: unbreakable rules
stated_reason: They recognize the validity of the countervailing considerations, yet find the standards usually cheap to implement and worth the effort.
quote: Moreover, we present these as strong heuristics rather than unbreakable rules—if an idea cannot be shared without violating these heuristics, we prefer the idea be shared and the heuristics set aside.
title: Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship

problem: How to demonstrate that claimed architectural improvements actually stem from the proposed innovations rather than other factors.
did: They cite the evaluation of Melis et al., which compared published architectures on equal footing with careful hyper-parameter tuning, showing vanilla LSTMs topped the leaderboard.
alternatives_named: attributing gains to complex architectural innovations
stated_reason: Without equal-footing comparisons, gains from hyper-parameter tuning are misattributed to architectural complexity.
quote: Recently, Melis et al. [54] demonstrated that a series of published improvements, originally attributed to complex innovations in network architectures, were actually due to better hyper-parameter tuning. On equal footing, vanilla LSTMs, hardly modified since 1997 [32], topped the leaderboard.
title: Troubling Trends in Machine Learning Scholarship

problem: How to evaluate pretrained models' knowledge without letting them exploit training-set artifacts or requiring large task-specific training sets.
did: They evaluated models only in zero-shot and few-shot (or transfer) settings, providing dev, val and test sets per task.
alternatives_named: fine-tuning on large in-distribution training sets
identically distributed training and test sets
stated_reason: The evaluation format differs from pretraining format, which obviates concerns about spurious training set annotation artifacts and enables a broader, more diverse set of tasks.
quote: Importantly, the format of our evaluation is not identical to the format in which information is acquired during pretraining. This has the benefit of obviating concerns about spurious training set annotation artifacts
title: Measuring Massive MultitaskLanguage Understanding

problem: How to measure language understanding in a way that is reliable and easy to score.
did: They used a multiple-choice classification accuracy test rather than natural language generation evaluation.
alternatives_named: Natural Language Generation evaluation
stated_reason: NLG is notoriously difficult to evaluate and lacks a standard metric.
quote: However, NLG is notoriously difficult to evaluate and lacks a standard metric (Sai et al., 2020). Consequently, we instead create a simple-to-evaluate test that measures classification accuracy on multiple choice questions.
title: Measuring Massive MultitaskLanguage Understanding

problem: What kind of benchmark would reveal model shortcomings when existing benchmarks were nearly saturated.
did: They built a benchmark of 57 subjects at elementary through professional difficulty, rather than commonsense or linguistic tasks.
alternatives_named: commonsense benchmarks
linguistic understanding benchmarks like GLUE/SuperGLUE
grade-school QA benchmarks
stated_reason: Near human-level performance on existing benchmarks suggests they do not capture important facets of language understanding.
quote: Overall, the near human-level performance on these benchmarks suggests that they are not capturing important facets of language understanding.
title: Measuring Massive MultitaskLanguage Understanding

problem: Whether the benefit of fine-tuning versus few-shot learning could be assessed on the test.
did: They additionally evaluated UnifiedQA, fine-tuned on other QA datasets, without further tuning, to measure transfer accuracy.
alternatives_named: few-shot GPT-3 only
further fine-tuning UnifiedQA on the test data
stated_reason: To test the usefulness of fine-tuning instead of few-shot learning.
quote: To test the usefulness of fine-tuning instead of few-shot learning, we also evaluate UnifiedQA models. UnifiedQA has the advantage of being fine-tuned on other question answering datasets, unlike GPT-3.
title: Measuring Massive MultitaskLanguage Understanding

problem: Whether high accuracy could be inflated by models memorizing exact test questions and answers from pretraining.
did: They checked the correlation between question log probability (entropy) and accuracy and concluded memorization was not evident.
stated_reason: Memorized questions should have low entropy and high accuracy, but the two were not positively correlated.
quote: However, in Figure 13, we see that accuracy and question entropy are not positively correlated, suggesting that the test's low-entropy questions do not correspond to memorized (and thereby correctly predicted) answers.
title: Measuring Massive MultitaskLanguage Understanding

problem: Why GPT-3 does poorly on calculation-heavy subjects despite apparently knowing relevant facts.
did: They probed whether GPT-3 knows the PEMDAS acronym and concluded it has declarative but not procedural knowledge, stating this as speculation.
stated_reason: GPT-3 knows the acronym PEMDAS but does not consistently apply it to actual problems.
quote: We speculate that is in part because GPT-3 acquires declarative knowledge more readily than procedural knowledge.
title: Measuring Massive MultitaskLanguage Understanding

problem: Whether a model's confidence can be trusted as a signal of correctness.
did: They measured calibration per subject, comparing average confidence to accuracy and computing RMS calibration error in zero-shot and few-shot settings.
stated_reason: A model's predictions should not be trusted unless its confidence is a good estimate of the probability of being correct.
quote: We evaluate the calibration of GPT-3 by testing how well its average confidence estimates its actual accuracy for each subject.
title: Measuring Massive MultitaskLanguage Understanding

problem: Whether specialized pretraining data can close the gap on Professional Law.
did: They continued pretraining RoBERTa on 1.6 million legal case summaries and fine-tuned on 2,000 collected law examples, then compared to the baseline.
alternatives_named: fine-tuning only on the custom law training set
stated_reason: To test the impact of additional specialized training data on performance.
quote: To test the impact of additional specialized training data, we also had RoBERTa continue pretraining on approximately 1.6 million legal case summaries using Harvard's Law Library case law corpus case.law, but after fine-tuning it only attained $36.1\%$ accuracy.
title: Measuring Massive MultitaskLanguage Understanding

problem: How to avoid being surprised by ML developments when forecasting future systems.
did: The author chose first-order forecasting, quantifying historical rates of progress and extrapolating, rather than intuitive zeroth-order forecasting.
alternatives_named: zeroth-order forecasting: looking at the current state of the art and adding improvements that feel reasonable
stated_reason: What seems reasonable is prone to cognitive bias and underestimates progress in a fast-moving field like ML.
quote: A more effective approach is first-order forecasting: quantifying the historical rate of progress and extrapolating it forward, while also considering reasons for possible slowdowns or speedups.
title: What will GPT-2030 look like?

problem: How to measure the inference speed of current models to ground a forecast.
did: The authors benchmarked models empirically by prompting them to count to n, cutting off at n tokens, and regressing time on tokens with a bias term for latency.
stated_reason: The bias term accounts for latency so the asymptotic tokens per second can be estimated.
quote: We then ran a linear regression with a bias term to account for latency in order to estimate the asymptotic number of tokens per second.
title: What will GPT-2030 look like?

problem: Human thinking speed estimates varied widely across measures (reading, speaking, listening, elliptic vs extended thought), so a benchmark had to be chosen.
did: The author chose 380 words per minute as the human thinking speed, since most numbers cluster in the 300-400 range.
alternatives_named: extended thought at ~4200 words per minute
reading, speaking and listening rates
stated_reason: Most of the numbers cluster in the 300-400 wpm range.
quote: Since most of these numbers cluster in the 300-400 wpm range, I’ll use 380 words per minute as my estimate of human thinking speed.
title: What will GPT-2030 look like?

problem: How confidently to state a forecast of model speed given conflicting trends.
did: The author gave a median of 5x human speed with a wide range and openly admitted deep uncertainty after studying trend data.
stated_reason: He was very uncertain how larger models versus better hardware and software would play out.
quote: I mostly concluded that I am very uncertain about how the competing trends of larger models vs. better hardware and software will play out.
title: What will GPT-2030 look like?

problem: How to bound the effect of running out of language data on the training-overhang forecast.
did: The author computed a pessimistic lower bound (high-quality data binding) and an upper bound (synthetic chain-of-thought data), then judged the lower bound too pessimistic and chose a central estimate.
alternatives_named: lower bound of an 8-fold increase from running out of high-quality data
upper bound of 300-fold from synthetic data
stated_reason: We will almost certainly find some way to leverage lower-quality or synthetic data.
quote: Overall, the lower bound seems fairly pessimistic to me as we’ll almost certainly find some way to leverage lower-quality or synthetic data.
title: What will GPT-2030 look like?

problem: Whether a naive ratio of Metaculus training compute to largest-model forward-pass cost is a valid estimate of training overhang.
did: The author rejected the naive ratio and used the Chinchilla scaling-based calculation instead.
alternatives_named: taking the ratio of Metaculus's training FLOPs to forward-pass FLOPs of the largest model
stated_reason: The largest model trained will likely not be state-of-the-art but something like the 174 trillion parameter BaGuaLu model.
quote: If we naively take the ratio, we again get 9e11 forward passes, but I think this is not the right calculation, because the largest model trained will likely not be state-of-the-art
title: What will GPT-2030 look like?

problem: How to communicate the reliability of the stated forecast ranges.
did: The author defined the ranges as 25th-75th percentiles and warned they are probably too narrow because only a mainline forecast was made.
stated_reason: He only did a mainline forecast without accounting for other options.
quote: In practice the range is probably too narrow because I only did a mainline forecast without accounting for “other” options.
title: What will GPT-2030 look like?

problem: How to interpret raw speed comparisons between humans and language models, given that words per minute is not like-for-like.
did: The author caveated that speed does not match quality and that GPT 2030 should be treated as a sped-up worker with a different skill profile rather than a sped-up human.
alternatives_named: treating GPT 2030 as a sped-up human
stated_reason: Speed is not necessarily matched by quality, and the model has a counterintuitive skill profile, failing at some easy tasks and mastering some difficult ones.
quote: We should therefore not think of GPT 2030 as a "sped-up human", but as a "sped-up worker" with a potentially counterintuitive skill profile.
title: What will GPT-2030 look like?

problem: How to show that a model's failure reflects a qualitative error mode rather than just lower accuracy on perturbed prompts.
did: They used a three-step design: build a semantics-preserving transformation, check that accuracy drops, then check that outputs contain elements indicative of the targeted failure.
alternatives_named: measuring only how frequently an error occurs
relying on complete mechanistic insight into the model
stated_reason: Open-ended outputs are syntactically diverse, so error rate alone is not descriptive, and the approach mirrors Tversky and Kahneman, who elicit failures without mechanistic insight.
quote: First, we construct a transformation over prompts that largely preserves semantics, but that we suspect will elicit a specific cognitive-bias-inspired failure mode. Next, we measure if code models are sensitive to the transformation, by measuring the decrease in accuracy.
title: Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases

problem: Whether the anchoring effect is explained by the model simply copying the anchor function verbatim.
did: They ran a control measuring verbatim copies of the anchor function and also renamed the anchor function so it differed from the function to be completed.
alternatives_named: shared function name between anchor and target function
stated_reason: To rule out verbatim copying and the shared function name as the cause of the anchoring results.
quote: One concern might be that models just outputs the anchor function verbatim, as in Section 3.3.1, but we find that this does not explain the full results—both models include anchor lines in many solutions that do not copy the anchor function verbatim.
title: Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases

problem: Whether the drop in accuracy on binary-first prompts is an artifact of the instructional style of the prompts.
did: They re-evaluated Codex on non-instructional prompts with the docstring beneath the function signature written as a definition.
alternatives_named: instructional prompts
stated_reason: To rule out that the dip in performance is due to the instructional nature of the prompts, and to mimic functions on GitHub more closely.
quote: One worry is that the dip in performance is due the instructional nature of our prompts. We rule this out by evaluating Codex on prompts where the docstring appears beneath the function signature and is a definition rather than command
title: Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases

problem: How to find candidate failure modes of open-ended generation models without mechanistic access to them.
did: They used human cognitive biases (framing, anchoring, availability, attribute substitution) as a reference system to generate hypotheses about model failures.
alternatives_named: other reference systems such as complex systems or evolution
intrinsic methods for characterizing model errors
stated_reason: Human cognitive biases are an analogous reference system that yields insights into ML systems, though models may also err in ways humans do not.
quote: This is an example of using a reference system—a system that is analogous to the ML models we study in some meaningful way—to generate insights into ML systems (Steinhardt, 2022).
title: Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases

problem: How to avoid confounds from option position and label when replicating the framing experiment on GPT-3.
did: They counterbalanced the risky option across labels A and B and across first and second position for every framing, population size, and save fraction.
stated_reason: To avoid the confounding influence of the position of the risky option and its label.
quote: To avoid the confounding influence of the position of the risky option and the label, for each prompt framing, population size, and save fraction we set the risky option to both option A and B, and put it both first and second.
title: Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases

problem: How strongly to claim GPT-3 exhibits anchoring given a small, templated replication with many gibberish outputs.
did: They disclosed the limitations of the replication and still stated a hedged conclusion that GPT-3 incorporates the anchor.
stated_reason: The original study also had a small sample, but 41% gibberish outputs and templated prompts limit the conclusions.
quote: Our replication has a few limitations. Like the original study our sample size is small, we construct prompts with templates, and many of the outputs—on average 41%—are gibberish. Nevertheless, our results suggest that GPT-3 incorporates the anchor during estimation.
title: Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases

problem: Whether to include CodeGen in all experiments or narrow to a single model when CodeGen's outputs were unusable.
did: They focused primarily on Codex for the availability, attribute substitution, and deletion experiments.
alternatives_named: running CodeGen on all prompt styles
stated_reason: CodeGen often produces nonsensical solutions on those prompt styles.
quote: We find that CodeGen often produces nonsensical solutions on the style of prompts used in Section 3.3.3, Section 3.3.4, and Section 5, so we focus primarily on Codex.
title: Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases

problem: How to interpret GPT-3's framing-effect results, which differ from humans at higher save probabilities.
did: They interpreted the divergence as potentially human-like, conjecturing that humans might behave similarly when the risky option is more certain, rather than as a failure.
stated_reason: For higher save probabilities the risky option is less risky, so choosing it under both framings is intuitive.
quote: However, for higher probabilities, GPT-3 consistently chooses the probabilistic option for both framings; we conjecture that humans could exhibit similar behavior in this regime, since the probabilistic option is more certain.
title: Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases

problem: How to interpret the descriptive-prompt deletion control, which showed more low-impact errors than the original prompts.
did: They interpreted the extra non-compiling outputs as evidence that the descriptive prompts may be more out-of-distribution, not as a contradiction of the main finding.
stated_reason: Instead of code that does something, the model produced code that fails to compile, while high-impact errors still appeared.
quote: This indicates that the prompt could actually be more out-of-distribution than the original prompts; instead of getting code that does something, we get code that fails to compile.
title: Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases

problem: How to test whether CCS recovers latent knowledge distinct from model outputs, when the model's outputs may be unreliable.
did: The authors added a prefix of incorrectly answered questions to the prompts to mislead model outputs and compared CCS against zero-shot accuracy.
stated_reason: Such a prefix should make the model imitate its context and answer incorrectly even if it internally knows better, giving a proof of concept that CCS works when outputs are unreliable.
quote: Specifically, we add a prefix to the beginning of our zero-shot prompts that consists of questions answered incorrectly (Figure 5). The hope is that such a prefix will decrease zero-shot accuracy
title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision

problem: How to interpret the effect of the misleading prefix, given that it behaved similarly with correct answers.
did: The authors acknowledged the ambiguity and visualized the top-100 output tokens with and without the prefix to check whether it truly induces false outputs.
alternatives_named: the prefix may instead reduce accuracy simply because it is out-of-distribution
stated_reason: To better understand what the prefix is doing despite the ambiguous interpretation.
quote: However, we found that results are qualitatively similar with correct answers, making the actual interpretation of the effect of this prefix ambiguous. Nevertheless, to better understand what this prefix is doing, we visualize the top $100$ tokens
title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision

problem: How to make a fair comparison between CCS and zero-shot when T0 was trained on most evaluation datasets.
did: The authors excluded T0 from the model averages because its zero-shot accuracy is inflated by training-data contamination.
stated_reason: T0 was trained on 9 of the 10 evaluation datasets, including some test data, so including it would give unfair comparisons.
quote: T0 was trained on 9 out of 10 of the datasets we evaluate on, including some of the data in our test splits, so we ignore it when averaging over models to avoid unfair comparisons.
title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision

problem: How to show CCS does not simply recover knowledge already present in the model's outputs.
did: The authors tested CCS on a masked language model with no [MASK] tokens and with the label placed mid-prompt, so outputs are uninformative, and verified that a modified zero-shot baseline performs much worse.
alternatives_named: last-layer hidden states right before the outputs
stated_reason: If CCS only worked when model outputs are useful, it should perform poorly in this setting.
quote: If CCS only works well when the model outputs are useful, then it should also perform poorly in this setting (as long as CCS uses the last-token hidden states as usual).
title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision

problem: Whether the CCS direction is dataset-specific rather than a general truth representation.
did: The authors trained CCS on one dataset and tested on every other, including ones with different label spaces, comparing against the no-transfer setting.
alternatives_named: training and testing on the same dataset (no transfer)
stated_reason: To rule out that the classifier captures dataset-specific properties such as which label is more likely correct.
quote: We rule this out by showing that it generalizes across completely different tasks, including ones with different label spaces (such as from “Yes” and “No” for a generic task to “Positive” and “Negative” for sentiment classification).
title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision

problem: Whether finding the CCS direction requires a large amount of unsupervised data.
did: The authors trained CCS on k unlabeled contrast pairs for k=1,2,4,..., resampling 32 times per k, using a single highest-zero-shot-accuracy prompt.
alternatives_named: training with the full training set and all prompts
stated_reason: To test whether strong performance comes from using lots of unsupervised data or whether the direction is easy to find.
quote: Whereas before we trained CCS using the full training set and all prompts, here we use limited data and a single prompt. Specifically, we train using only $k$ unlabeled contrast pairs
title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision

problem: Whether the truth direction can be found by simpler methods than CCS, to assess how salient truth is.
did: The authors introduced Contrastive Representation Clustering variants (top principal component and bimodal salience search) and compared them with CCS.
alternatives_named: top principal component thresholding
bimodal salience search
stated_reason: If simple clustering of contrast-pair differences works, truth representations are salient and relatively easy to find.
quote: We compare CCS and these two variants of Contrastive Representation Clustering in Table 2, using the same setting as in Table 1. While CCS performs best, all methods attain high accuracy and are competitive with zero-shot performance.
title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision

problem: How to make the zero-shot baseline strong enough for a fair comparison with CCS.
did: The authors calibrated zero-shot predictions to be balanced 50/50 and reported calibrated accuracy by default, and used an NLI-finetuned zero-shot baseline for encoder-only models.
alternatives_named: uncalibrated zero-shot
stated_reason: Zero-shot outputs suffer from miscalibration, and calibration raises accuracy by about 5% on average.
quote: We use a variant of the calibration method presented in Zhao et al. (2021) by balancing predictions to be 50/50 across the two output labels.
title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision

problem: How strongly to claim statistical significance of the main accuracy comparisons given correlated samples.
did: The authors computed a coarse upper bound on standard error using only the independent examples, applied a Wald test, and flagged minor observations such as CCS (All Data) vs CCS as not necessarily significant.
alternatives_named: more powerful but complicated statistical tests
stated_reason: Ignoring averaging over correlated prompts and models gives a conservative bound, and more powerful tests would only give smaller p-values.
quote: Some minor observations are not necessarily statistically significant, such as that CCS (All Data) outperforms CCS on average (Section 3.2.1), but none of these are important for our main claims
title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision

problem: How to define the toxicity component of the auditing objective so that optimization yields solutions faithful to the target behavior rather than exploiting classifier weaknesses.
did: They defined toxicity with a unigram model over per-token toxicity probabilities instead of plugging a neural toxicity classifier directly into the objective.
alternatives_named: directly use neural toxicity models in the objective
stated_reason: Neural toxicity classifiers were found to be susceptible to hacking: the optimizer returned solutions that fooled the classifier but were not faithful to the target behavior.
quote: We do not directly use neural toxicity models in the objective, since we find that they are susceptible to hacking: our optimizer returns solutions that fool the toxicity classifier, but are not faithful to the target behavior.
title: Automatically Auditing Large Language Models via Discrete Optimization

problem: Whether to optimize only over prompts or jointly over prompts and outputs when searching for audit examples.
did: They formulated the problem as joint optimization over prompt and output, adding the output log-probability as a differentiable surrogate for the greedy-decoding constraint.
alternatives_named: only optimize over prompts (optimize phi(x,f(x)))
stated_reason: Joint optimization lets them update the output directly to match target behavior rather than indirectly through the prompt, which matters for rare behaviors with limited optimization signal.
quote: However, joint optimization allows us to more directly optimize for output behaviors; we can update $o$ directly to match the target output behavior, rather than indirectly updating $f(x)$ through the prompt.
title: Automatically Auditing Large Language Models via Discrete Optimization

problem: How to measure optimizer success fairly when some target outputs may be impossible to produce via greedy decoding.
did: They reported a normalized success rate restricted to outputs for which any run of any optimizer found a satisfactory prompt, alongside the raw success rate.
stated_reason: Some failures may be inevitable because outputs may not be greedily generatable, so raw success rates understate optimizer performance.
quote: We therefore also compute a normalized success rate: the success rate over outputs where any run of any optimizer produces a satisfactory prompt. We plot this normalized score as a dashed line in Figure 1.
title: Automatically Auditing Large Language Models via Discrete Optimization

problem: How to compare the proposed optimizer against existing methods across tasks and model sizes in a controlled way.
did: They compared ARCA against AutoPrompt and GBDA on the same tasks, with five random seeds per output, multiple prompt/output lengths, and compute-matched GBDA runs.
stated_reason: Averaging over random seeds and lengths gives a reliable success rate, and batching GBDA runs makes computational cost comparable.
quote: For each output, we run each optimizer five times with different random seeds, and report the average success rate over all runs.
title: Automatically Auditing Large Language Models via Discrete Optimization

problem: How to interpret why ARCA outperforms AutoPrompt in different settings (fixed output vs jointly optimized output).
did: They attributed the gain in the fixed-output setting to averaging random first-order approximations, and the gain in the joint setting to the autoregressive term.
stated_reason: When the output is fixed the autoregressive term does not influence the ranking, so only averaging can explain the difference.
quote: The improvement of ARCA over AutoPrompt comes from averaging random first-order approximations; the output is fixed, so the autoregressive term does not influence the ranking.
title: Automatically Auditing Large Language Models via Discrete Optimization

problem: How to test whether the prompts found by auditing a small model reveal failures in larger, differently trained models.
did: They ran a small transfer study, feeding 100 GPT-2-found three-token prompts to GPT-3 davinci-002 and measuring identical outputs, matching first tokens, and manually inspected toxicity.
alternatives_named: direct optimization on the larger model
stated_reason: Prompt transfer matters when model access is restricted (e.g. API only) or direct optimization is computationally intractable.
quote: we conduct a small quantitative study where we sample 100 three-token prompts that GPT-2 completes to two-token toxic comments, and input them to GPT-3 davinci-002.
title: Automatically Auditing Large Language Models via Discrete Optimization

problem: How to test whether auditing a better model yields more natural prompts without confounding from explicit naturalness supervision.
did: They omitted the perplexity loss, sampled 100 prompts per length for GPT-2 and GPT-J, and compared their mean log-perplexity under GPT-3 davinci-002 plus qualitative inspection.
alternatives_named: include a perplexity loss in the objective
stated_reason: Removing explicit naturalness supervision isolates the effect of scaling the audited model, without confounders.
quote: The point of these results is to test how scaling the model we audit increases naturalness, without confounders.
title: Automatically Auditing Large Language Models via Discrete Optimization

problem: How strongly to claim that the prompt transfer and naturalness results generalize.
did: They described the transfer and naturalness studies as small-scale and framed the results as evidence rather than proof.
stated_reason: The studies are small, so they only provide evidence that auditing tools become more powerful as systems improve.
quote: These results provide evidence that as systems improve, our auditing tools can simultaneously become more powerful.
title: Automatically Auditing Large Language Models via Discrete Optimization

problem: Whether to audit with the objective as a pre-deployment search or to use the objective as an inference-time filter.
did: They chose pre-deployment auditing via optimization over filtering outputs by the auditing objective.
alternatives_named: use phi to filter prompts at inference
stated_reason: Filtering rejects false positives that can harm subgroups, can be unacceptable when outputs are time-sensitive, and only partially covers failures.
quote: Filtering excludes false positives—examples where $\phi(x,o)$ is erroneously high that are fine to generate—which can disproportionately harm subgroups [Xu et al., 2021a].
title: Automatically Auditing Large Language Models via Discrete Optimization

problem: How to evaluate XPT forecasters whose forecasts only covered 2024 and 2030, so they cannot be directly resolved against 2023 outcomes.
did: Used proxy criteria: whether progress already exceeds the 2024 forecast, whether extrapolated trends make it implausible, and divergence from the current Metaculus 2024 forecast.
alternatives_named: fully resolving the XPT forecasters against a 2023 outcome
stated_reason: The tournament did not ask for 2023 forecasts, and Metaculus has a year of extra data and did well last year, so it is reasonable to trust it.
quote: If the 2024 forecast diverges significantly from the current Metaculus forecast for 2024, then the forecast is arguably bad. The justification for this is that the current Metaculus forecast has a year of extra data so is better-informed, and Metaculus did well last year so it is reasonable to trust them.
title: AI Forecasting: Two Years In

problem: How to assess whether XPT 2024 forecasts are too narrow when reality for 2024 is not yet observable.
did: Computed the probability, under the 2023 Metaculus forecast, that reality exceeds each group's 95th percentile as a proxy for reality.
alternatives_named: waiting for actual 2024 results
stated_reason: Metaculus has a year of extra data and so should be closer to reality than the 2022 forecasts.
quote: Since we don't have access to reality (it isn't 2024 yet), as a proxy I'll compute the probability (under the Metaculus 2023 forecast) that each of these forecasts exceed their 95th percentile.
title: AI Forecasting: Two Years In

problem: How to interpret the expert vs. superforecaster performance gap, which reversed the author's impressions from the prior year.
did: Attributed the difference partly to selection effects and partly to effort and incentives (formal quantitative predictions with monetary incentive vs. informal hallway conversations), and concluded experts can be trusted more in this setting.
alternatives_named: selection effects (experts who try to register forecasts are more likely to be correct)
stated_reason: Last year's expert 'forecasts' were informal hallway conversations, whereas this year they were formal quantitative predictions with some monetary incentive.
quote: But I'd guess some is also effort: the expert "forecasts" I had in mind last year were from informal hallway conversations, while this year they were formal quantitative predictions with some (small) monetary incentive to be correct.
title: AI Forecasting: Two Years In

problem: Whether a good bottom-line forecast reflects a correct understanding of the drivers of progress.
did: Evaluated the author's own preregistered reasoning by checking specific claimed sources of improvement against what actually happened, not just the final probabilities.
alternatives_named: judging only the bottom-line forecast
stated_reason: A good final forecast could still hide an incorrect picture of the situation, e.g. if improvement came from scaling rather than prompt engineering.
quote: Since I included public reasoning for my own forecast, we can go beyond the bottom-line probabilities and look at whether I got things right for the right reasons.
title: AI Forecasting: Two Years In

problem: How to explain the unexplained portion of the 18% MATH accuracy gain from Let's Verify Step by Step.
did: Hypothesized that chain-of-thought distillation (fine-tuning on filtered step-by-step solutions) accounted for about 8%, citing similar prior work.
alternatives_named: fine-tuning on more data
improved majority vote aggregation
stated_reason: Though intended only to teach format, previous work (Huang et al. 2022) shows chain-of-thought distillation can significantly improve accuracy, e.g. GSM-8K from 74% to 82%.
quote: Even though it was not intended to improve accuracy, previous work shows that this type of chain-of-thought distillation can improve accuracy significantly: Huang et al. (2022) apply a similar technique to improve performance on GSM-8K from 74% to 82%.
title: AI Forecasting: Two Years In

problem: Whether to count majority-vote improvement and undocumented MMLU improvements as resolving the forecast.
did: Followed the resolution rules strictly, excluding the disqualified majority-vote result and improvements not formally documented for MMLU.
alternatives_named: counting the majority-vote result from Let's Verify
counting undocumented improvements to MMLU
stated_reason: The majority-vote result used non-allowed training data, and undocumented MMLU improvements do not affect forecast resolution.
quote: In fact, the only major improvement that didn't happen was "improving over majority vote", which was in the Let's Verify paper and improved performance by about 10%, but was disqualified due to using non-allowed data to train.
title: AI Forecasting: Two Years In

problem: How strongly to conclude that superforecasters were miscalibrated, given that their initial-stage MATH forecast missed Minerva.
did: Treated the Minerva miss as further evidence of miscalibration while hedging that forecasters may have run out of time and experts may have simply known of Minerva.
alternatives_named: attributing the miss to forecasters running out of time
experts simply being aware of the Minerva result
stated_reason: The superforecasters' 95th percentile was 55% because they failed to predict Minerva, but timing and awareness confounds make the evidence suggestive only.
quote: This could partly be due to forecasters running out of time in the initial stage, but nevertheless shows that they had miscalibrated intuitions.
title: AI Forecasting: Two Years In

problem: How strongly to claim the forecaster ranking and the quality of the author's own forecasting given only two benchmarks.
did: Stated that the author can make reasonable forecasts and that Metaculus did well, while explicitly caveating the small sample of N=2 and using hedged language like 'probably' for the XPT groups.
stated_reason: The sample is only two benchmarks, though the reasoning also held up beyond the bottom-line forecast.
quote: Metaculus continues to fare well on AI benchmark forecasts, and I've shown that I can make reasonable forecasts as well (with the caveat of N=2, but the reasoning holds up in addition to the bottom-line forecast).
title: AI Forecasting: Two Years In

problem: How to guard against the evaluation being overfit to the authors' own attack-design prompts and to ensure generalization of attack success.
did: They built a larger synthetic dataset of 317 prompts that was held out, not used to design attacks, and not seen by the authors until after data collection, and evaluated only the top attacks on it.
alternatives_named: evaluating only on the curated dataset
stated_reason: To maximize statistical validity and to show the attacks are not specifically adapted to the curated dataset.
quote: To maximize statistical validity, the dataset was not used to design attacks and was not seen by the authors until after data collection.
title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?

problem: How to test whether the specific content of the prefix injection and refusal suppression attacks, rather than just the attack format, causes the jailbreaks to work.
did: They ran ablations: swapping the injected prefix to "Hello!" and inverting the refusal suppression rules, and compared them to the full attacks.
stated_reason: To support the claim that the specific prefix injected and the specific instructions are important for the success of these jailbreaks.
quote: Table 1 verifies the hypotheses of Section 3: prefix_injection outperforms its ablation prefix_injection_hello, and refusal_suppression outperforms its ablation refusal_suppression_inv.
title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?

problem: How to establish a baseline so that attack success can be attributed to the jailbreak rather than to the prompts being innocuous.
did: They included a none control that echoes each prompt verbatim, and also a harmless control prompt to check that the model can still answer under each attack.
stated_reason: A very low Bad Bot rate for the control confirms the prompts are indeed unsafe; the harmless prompt checks basic question-answering capability under attacks.
quote: We also verify that the control jailbreak none has a very low Bad Bot\xspace rate, further confirming that these prompts are indeed unsafe.
title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?

problem: How to score model outputs when responses may be obfuscated, encoded with errors, or ambiguous in whether they are harmful and on topic.
did: The authors manually labeled all outputs using a fixed rubric into Good Bot, Bad Bot, or Unclear, rather than using automated classifiers.
alternatives_named: automated labeling
stated_reason: Many outputs can be obfuscated or encoded with errors, and the data contained harmful content, so the authors labeled consistently by hand following a fixed scheme.
quote: We evaluate results by hand as many outputs can be obfuscated or encoded with errors. To ensure consistency, we exactly follow the labeling scheme specified in Appendix B.
title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?

problem: How to reduce noise from model updates and stochastic decoding when comparing attacks on API-served models.
did: They collected data for each model within a 6-day window, sampled at temperature 0, randomized query order, and later checked robustness with temperature 1 on the strongest attacks.
alternatives_named: temperature 1 sampling
stated_reason: To minimize the impact of incremental model updates and decoding noise, and to ensure unbiased comparisons between attacks even if the underlying model changes.
quote: We randomize query order within each experiment run to ensure unbiased comparisons between attacks even if the underlying model changes.
title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?

problem: How to interpret GPT-3.5 Turbo's low success on complex attacks like the combination and Base64 attacks, which could mean robustness or simply inability to understand the input.
did: They interpreted the high Unclear rates and failed harmless control prompts as a lack of capability, concluding that some vulnerabilities only emerge at sufficient scale.
alternatives_named: GPT-3.5 Turbo being robust to these attacks
stated_reason: Base64 examples were Unclear at a high rate and harmless control prompts did not succeed, indicating the model cannot understand complex inputs.
quote: We identify this as GPT-3.5 Turbo not having the capability to understand complex inputs: evidence comes from the Base64 examples being Unclear\xspace at a high rate and the harmless control prompts not succeeding
title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?

problem: How to simulate a motivated attacker who can choose among attacks to measure worst-case vulnerability.
did: They defined an adaptive attack that counts a prompt as broken if any of the evaluated attacks succeeds on it.
stated_reason: To simulate an adaptive adversary who can choose the attack based on the prompt.
quote: To simulate an adaptive adversary who can choose the attack based on the prompt, we consider a simple "adaptive" attack that succeeds if any of the 28 evaluated attacks succeed.
title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?

problem: How strongly to state conclusions about the defense implications of scaling given that only black-box access to proprietary models was available.
did: They argued scaling alone will not resolve the failure modes and safety-capability parity is necessary, while acknowledging in the limitations that confirmation of their hypotheses is only indirect.
alternatives_named: white-box study
mechanistic interpretation
stated_reason: Due to the proprietary nature of GPT-4 and Claude, the authors are limited to indirect confirmation of their hypotheses.
quote: Due to the proprietary nature of state-of-the-art LLMs like GPT-4 and Claude, we are limited to indirect confirmation of our hypotheses.
title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?

problem: How to select representative popular existing jailbreaks for comparison against the newly designed attacks without cherry-picking.
did: They chose the top two attacks on jailbreakchat.com each by "Votes" and "JB score" on a fixed date (April 13, 2023).
stated_reason: To select the best popular jailbreaks for comparison.
quote: To select the best popular jailbreaks, we chose the top two attacks on April 13, 2023 each in terms of "Votes" and "JB score" [3].
title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?

problem: How to simulate real-time forecasting on already-resolved questions without leaking outcome information through the choice of retrieval dates.
did: They chose retrieval dates on a geometric schedule between open and close dates rather than relative to the resolve date.
alternatives_named: retrieving at geometric intervals between the open and resolve date
stated_reason: Choosing dates relative to the resolve date would leak information because the resolve date correlates with the resolution.
quote: It is tempting to choose retrieval dates with respect to the resolve date so that each question can receive the same number of retrieval dates, e.g. by retrieving at geometric intervals between the open and resolve date.
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models

problem: How to prevent leakage from pre-training and tuning when building the train, validation and test splits.
did: They put only post-cut-off questions in the test set, resolved train/validation questions before the cut-off, and discarded questions spanning the date.
stated_reason: To guard against leakage from LMs' pre-training and from the tuning process.
quote: All test set questions were opened after the date, and all train and validation questions were resolved before. Questions that span across the date are discarded.
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models

problem: Whether post-training could leak knowledge of events after the stated knowledge cut-offs of the models used.
did: They manually queried the models on 20 major post-cut-off events, plus a sanity check on 20 pre-cut-off events, before trusting the cut-off dates.
stated_reason: To check that post-training does not leak information past the knowledge cut-off.
quote: As a test, we manually query the model on $20$ major events in June, 2023--September, 2023 3 3 3 sourced from https://www.onthisday.com/events/date/2023/., such as “Who won the 2023 Turkish presidential election?”.
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models

problem: How to establish a fair baseline of unaided LM forecasting ability before building the system.
did: They evaluated all 14 LMs with zero-shot and scratchpad prompts, picking the best prompt per strategy on the validation set and reporting test scores, with no retrieval.
alternatives_named: no additional information retrieval
stated_reason: To show models are not naturally good at forecasting and that retrieval and tuning are needed.
quote: For each prompting strategy, we craft candidate prompts, pick the best prompt on the validation set, and report its Brier scores on the test set.
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models

problem: How to choose hyperparameters without tuning on the test set or confounding the sweeps.
did: They swept hyperparameter groups sequentially on the validation set, fixing earlier optima and randomizing unswept ones per question.
stated_reason: For efficiency and to avoid confounding between hyperparameters.
quote: We optimize the groups sequentially, fixing the optimal configurations from previous groups while sweeping the current one. The hyperparameters yet to be swept are randomized independently for each input question.
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models

problem: How to cheaply rate article relevance when full texts are too costly.
did: They compared title-only, title plus first 250 words, and embedding similarity against GPT-4 full-text gold labels, and chose title plus first 250 words.
alternatives_named: Title-only
Embedding similarity
full article texts
stated_reason: Title-only can mislead on failed scrapes; title plus 250 words had the highest precision at recall above 70% and saved about 70% of cost.
quote: In sum, fixing recall at above $70\%$, querying GPT-3.5-Turbo with title + first $250$ words attains the highest precision.
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models

problem: How to avoid fine-tuning on forecasts that outperform the crowd by luck or that would induce overconfidence.
did: They kept only outputs beating the crowd's Brier score, discarded those deviating by more than 0.15 from the crowd, and averaged targets with the crowd prediction.
stated_reason: Selecting only outputs that beat the crowd can inadvertently cause overconfidence in the fine-tuned model.
quote: To mitigate this, we discard pairs where the prediction deviates by more than $0.15$ from the crowd prediction, and we also average our prediction with the crowd prediction when constructing the target output.
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models

problem: How to explain why the system underperforms the crowd on confident questions and at later retrieval dates.
did: They hypothesized the system hedges because of safety training and supported it with an accuracy-versus-Brier comparison on high-certainty questions.
stated_reason: The system rarely outputs low probabilities, and accuracy is higher while Brier score is worse, consistent with hedging.
quote: We hypothesize that this stems from our model’s tendency to hedge predictions due to its safety training (see Figure 17 for a qualitative example).
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models

problem: How strongly to state conclusions from per-category differences in the results.
did: They cautioned against drawing strong conclusions from subcategory variation.
stated_reason: Subcategory sample sizes are smaller, so variation could be due to noise.
quote: However, we caution against drawing strong conclusions from subcategories, since the sample size is smaller and variation could be due to noise.
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models

problem: Whether the system's gains depend on GPT-4's power, and how much each component (fine-tuning, retrieval) contributes.
did: They ran three ablations: fine-tuned GPT-3.5 instead of GPT-4, no fine-tuning, and no fine-tuning plus no retrieval.
alternatives_named: fine-tuned GPT-3.5
base GPT-4 only
no retrieval
stated_reason: To validate that performance is not solely due to GPT-4 and to show the benefits of retrieval and fine-tuning.
quote: We conduct $3$ ablation studies. The first validates that our performance is not solely due to the power of GPT-4. The last two show the benefits of our retrieval and fine-tuning methods.
title: Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models

problem: How to validate the full SFT/DPO/Frank-Wolfe pipeline in a setting where success can be measured against a known answer.
did: They built a test set of 4096 gold (prefix, suffix) pairs from FineWeb and checked whether the investigator recovers prefixes whose elicitation score is at least as high as the gold prefix, without DPO/FW ever seeing the gold prefix.
stated_reason: It tests the entire pipeline in a simplified setting where the result can be compared to known ground-truth, and the algorithm never sees test set labels.
quote: We use this to test our entire pipeline in a simplified setting where we can compare to known ground-truth.
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

problem: Whether the strong jailbreak results from a WildChat-trained investigator reflect the method or merely human-written attacks leaked in the SFT prior.
did: They ran a control ablation using UltraChat, an entirely synthetic instruction dataset, for supervised fine-tuning and checked whether success remained high.
alternatives_named: WildChat
stated_reason: WildChat might contain human-constructed attacks that could aid an investigator in attacking a target LM, so the control rules this out.
quote: We use WildChat for the majority of our experiments, since it contains diverse, natural propmts; however, it might also contain instances of human-constructed attacks that could aid an investigator in attacking a target LM. To control for this,
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

problem: Whether to infer the prompt directly from the rubric verifier score or to decompose rubric elicitation into stages.
did: They adopted a two-stage approach (infer response y from rubric, then prompt x from y) after finding one-stage DPO performed significantly worse.
alternatives_named: one-stage DPO directly optimizing prompts based on the verifier score
stated_reason: One-stage DPO performed significantly worse than two-stage DPO in early experiments and in the in-distribution benchmark.
quote: In early experiments, we tried a one-stage approach to rubric elicitation where we directly optimize prompts $x$ based on the verifier score. We found this to perform significantly worse than two-stage DPO (Appendix A.5), so we used our two-stage approach in all our experiments.
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

problem: How to handle plain DPO collapsing to a low-entropy repetition strategy, which makes it a poor basis for diversity.
did: They treated mode collapse as a failure to be fixed and introduced an iterative Frank-Wolfe procedure that penalizes prompts found in earlier iterations.
alternatives_named: simply applying DPO
stated_reason: DPO runs learn to repeat the suffix, exploiting the repetition bias in transformers, whereas the authors want a wider range of successful strategies.
quote: However, simply applying DPO often leads to mode collapse, a phenomenon which decreases the sample diversity of a model (Song et al., 2023). For example, we observe that some DPO runs learn to primarily generate prompts that repeat the suffix
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

problem: Which DPO iterate to use as the regularizer in Frank-Wolfe when the best-scoring iterate has very low entropy.
did: They used the 2nd of 15 DPO iterations as the regularizer for later rounds instead of the best-scoring iterate.
alternatives_named: the best DPO iterate by elicitation score
stated_reason: The best iterate sometimes has very low entropy, making it an ineffective regularizer, while the 2nd iterate uses a similar qualitative strategy with higher entropy.
quote: We find that the resulting DPO iterate sometimes has very low entropy, making it an ineffective regularizer for Frank-Wolfe; to address this, we use the 2nd (out of 15) iteration of DPO as the regularizer for future rounds
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

problem: How to prevent the jailbreak investigator from reward hacking by satisfying the affirmative-prefix target without producing actually harmful output.
did: They augmented the DPO reward with a Llama-3.1 8B harmfulness judge and also required the next token not be EOS.
alternatives_named: targeting only the affirmative response string
stated_reason: To alleviate reward hacking, i.e. to check that responses are actually harmful.
quote: To alleviate reward hacking, we also augment the DPO reward with a Llama-3.1 8B judge to check that responses are actually harmful (see Appendix F for details).
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

problem: How strongly to claim superiority over GCG given that the published GCG numbers come from a different setup.
did: They reported GCG numbers from the original paper but explicitly flagged them as not directly comparable (different model and test split), and noted grader false positives.
stated_reason: Zou et al. attack Llama 2 and use a different test data split, so the comparison is not apples to apples.
quote: *GCG numbers are not directly comparable, as Zou et al. (2023) attack Llama 2 and use a different test data split. Success rate for Adaptive Attacks is taken from Andriushchenko et al..
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

problem: How to assess whether elicited attacks are useful beyond the single target model they were optimized against.
did: They tested transfer of best-of-25 attacks from a Llama-3.1 8B investigator to larger Llama models and closed-weight models like GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
stated_reason: To see whether attacks generalize to non-target models.
quote: We further test the transfer of our attacks to models other than Llama-3.1 8B, reporting results in Table 5. We find very high transfer to larger models in the Llama family as well as some transfer even to closed-weight models such as GPT-4o and Claude 3.5.
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

problem: How to set the step-size schedule for aggregating Frank-Wolfe iterates, given the canonical choice differs from simple averaging.
did: They compared the canonical eta_i = 2/(i+1) against uniform averaging eta_i = 1/i and chose uniform averaging.
alternatives_named: eta_i = 2/(i+1) canonical Frank-Wolfe step size
stated_reason: Uniform averaging converged to a better overall objective L and gave better diversity, at a slight cost in fluency and elicitation.
quote: As shown in Figure 6, we find that setting $\eta_{i}=\frac{1}{i}$ converges to a better objective $\mathcal{L}$. It outperforms $\eta_{i}=\frac{2}{u_{1}}$ in terms of diversity score, while performing slightly worse on fluency and elicitation.
title: Eliciting Language Model Behaviors with Investigator Agents

problem: Training a decoder on naively constructed LatentQA data could let it shortcut by reading the control tokens directly instead of learning to decode latent properties.
did: They sometimes mask the control activations and provide only stimulus activations during training.
alternatives_named: train the decoder on activations from both the control and stimulus tokens
stated_reason: The decoder may learn to cheat by directly reading the control token embeddings present in the residual stream of the control token activations.
quote: A straightforward approach would be to train the decoder on activations from both the control and stimulus tokens. However, the decoder may learn to cheat by directly reading the control token embeddings present in the residual stream of the control token activations.
title: LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to DecodeActivations Into Natural Language

problem: How to choose the target-model layer to read from and the decoder layer to write to without an a priori basis.
did: They ran a hyperparameter sweep over read and write layers, scoring each by lowest test loss on a held-out evaluation set, and used the best configuration for all experiments.
stated_reason: The k=15, l=0 configuration had the best generalization on the evaluation dataset.
quote: We evaluate each configuration by measuring the lowest test loss on the evaluation dataset described in Section 5.3. We report results in Table 6 and find that the $k=15$ and $\ell=0$ has the best generalization.
title: LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to DecodeActivations Into Natural Language

problem: How to evaluate whether the decoder generalizes to personas it has not seen, given the hidden-system-prompt reading task.
did: They ensured the evaluation personas did not appear in the decoder's training data.
stated_reason: To test generalization.
quote: We study two settings: an easy setting with a list of 25 personas (composed of fictional characters, scientists, and political figures) and a hard setting with a list of 25 personas (composed of only scientists). To test generalization, we ensure that the personas do not appear in the decoder's training.
title: LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to DecodeActivations Into Natural Language

problem: Which baselines to compare against fairly on the hidden system prompt task, where linear probing is not applicable and GPT-4 sees different information.
did: They compared against SelfIE and a stronger GPT-4 prompting baseline given the full user-assistant dialog, and gave all methods additional dialogs as extra context if the first attempt failed.
alternatives_named: linear probing
stated_reason: Linear probing requires prior knowledge of the personas, so it is not applicable.
quote: We also compare to prompting GPT-4, 1 1 1 In this setting, linear probing is not applicable since it requires prior knowledge of the personas. This highlights the flexibility of LatentQA over linear probing.
title: LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to DecodeActivations Into Natural Language

problem: Choosing a fair comparison between the decoder's activation-based steering and RepE, which offers two control variants.
did: They used RepE's training-based LoRRA finetuning variant rather than its training-free steering vector method for the debiasing comparison.
alternatives_named: RepE training-free method that adds steering vectors to activations
stated_reason: For a fair comparison.
quote: For RepE, we use the training-based method (called LoRRA finetuning) for a fair comparison. We finetune with the prompts "Pretend you are an unbiased/biased person," with stimulus activations from the Alpaca instruction-tuning dataset
title: LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to DecodeActivations Into Natural Language

problem: RepE increased the log-likelihood difference in debiasing, which is an unexpected result needing explanation.
did: They interpreted it as RepE overshooting equality and hypothesized that bias is not linearly represented, while the decoder handles nonlinear concepts.
stated_reason: A concept such as bias may not be linearly represented, yet RepE steers towards linear concepts.
quote: In fact, RepE actually increases the log-likelihood difference, because it downweights the probability of stereotyped sentences and upweights the probability of non-stereotyped sentences past the point of equality. We suspect this is because a concept such as bias may not be linearly represented
title: LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to DecodeActivations Into Natural Language

problem: Because there is no ground truth for latents, the decoder's outputs might be hallucinated, so it is unclear whether to trust its fidelity.
did: They argued indirectly for reliability from competitive reading performance and successful counterfactual steering, rather than direct ground-truth validation.
stated_reason: The method would not achieve competitive reading performance if it were hallucinating, and its steering shows it decodes concepts correctly enough to counterfactually steer.
quote: Second, because we have no ground truth for latents, our decoder may hallucinate. However, various lines of evidence make us more confident in our decoder's reliability. For example, our method would not be able to achieve competitive performance on reading tasks if it were hallucinating.
title: LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to DecodeActivations Into Natural Language

problem: Whether lower evaluation loss with scale translates into real downstream gains, rather than only a loss-based scaling trend.
did: They replicated the scaling experiment on a downstream task by training on smaller Llama models and re-running the hidden system prompt experiment.
alternatives_named: relying on loss curves alone
stated_reason: To confirm that improvements in evaluation loss translate to meaningful gains on downstream LatentQA tasks.
quote: We replicate the scaling experiment from Figure 11 by evaluating downstream task performance across model sizes. We train Lit on Llama-3.2-1B and Llama-3.2-3B and re-run the uncovering hidden system prompts experiment (Section 5.1).
title: LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to DecodeActivations Into Natural Language

problem: Whether the method's reading and control results hold beyond one model family and architecture.
did: They trained a decoder on Gemma-3-4b-it and re-ran the hidden system prompt and debiasing experiments.
stated_reason: To show the approach applies across different architectures and training paradigms.
quote: To show that our LatentQA decoder for Gemma-3-4b-it is effective, we show that it can do reading and control. In particular, we re-run the "uncovering hidden system prompts" reading experiment (Section 5.1)
title: LatentQA: Teaching LLMs to DecodeActivations Into Natural Language

problem: Whether the trained investigator beats an established automated jailbreak method.
did: They ran Best-of-N Jailbreaking against GPT-4.1 as a baseline, using the same judge as the RL runs, and compared it to a black-box-trained investigator.
alternatives_named: Best-of-N Jailbreaking
stated_reason: It is a strong red-teaming baseline for comparison.
quote: We also compare our approach to a strong red-teaming baseline, Best-of-N Jailbreaking [3]. When optimizing Best-of-N Jailbreaking solely for GPT-4.1, we find that it achieves a 5% pass@1 and 63% pass@32 on GPT-4.1
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

problem: Black-box rewards worked well here despite performing poorly in the authors' earlier work.
did: They attributed the success to the task dataset, which spans related tasks of varying difficulty and so acts as a natural curriculum for RL.
stated_reason: A spectrum of related tasks of varying difficulty gives a good RL curriculum; this is stated as speculation.
quote: We were initially surprised that black-box rewards worked so well here, as they performed much worse in our previous work on eliciting self-harm behaviors [2]. We speculate that this is because our dataset of CBRN tasks contains a spectrum of related tasks of varying degrees of difficulty, providing a good curriculum for RL.
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

problem: How much to invest in training against the most expensive flagship target models.
did: They limited experiments on the flagship models because of API cost.
stated_reason: Black-box training against flagship models can cost up to $5,000-$10,000.
quote: For flagship models (GPT-5-thinking, Claude Opus 4.1), this can increase to up to $5,000-$10,000, so we performed limited experiments on them.
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

problem: Whether to extend the approach to other kinds of harmful tasks beyond the curated set.
did: They did not pursue tasks for which they could not build a reliable judge, and flagged this as a limitation.
stated_reason: RL-based red-teaming needs robust judges to avoid reward-hacking, and some behaviors are context-dependent.
quote: we had difficulty constructing judges for other tasks, such as the model writing code implementing malicious exploits (which might be allowed in legitimate educational contexts).
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

problem: Whether attacks learned against one accessible model carry over to other models.
did: They trained on individual models, such as the open-weight GPT-oss-20b alone, and measured how the attacks transferred to the other targets.
alternatives_named: optimizing a weighted sum of rewards across multiple models
stated_reason: Training on less robust models may give a useful intermediate signal for attacking more robust ones.
quote: Attacks often transfer. In particular, solely optimizing attack success for GPT-oss-20b still leads to strong transfer to other language models. This is true for both the PRBO and black-box objectives.
title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents | Transluce AI

problem: Why the two most resilient targets showed much lower success rates.
did: They interpreted the low rates as partly due to the additional monitoring layers, noting that the attacks plainly requested harmful content and were easily detected, and left bypassing the guardrails to future work.
alternatives_named: designing an output encoding scheme that goes undetected by response monitors
generating attacks against an open-weight monitor and relying on transfer
